plan.topic: A quick sting or sore spot during or right after a tirzepatide pen shot: is that normal, what the label counts as an injection-site reaction, and when to call
plan.angle:
08:00 calm 'Is this normal?' pen moment. Follow the task's length arm and hook archetype.
- Sentence 1 (14 words or fewer): 'Tirzepatide shot stung for a second? The label counts injection-site reactions.' Scene 1's on-screen text matches it.
- Relief fact in the same sentence or the next, no standalone validation line: injection-site reactions were reported in 6–8% by dose vs about 2% on placebo (Zepbound PI rev. 28 Aug 2026, section 6.1). Population on the card: adults with obesity, or overweight plus at least one weight-related condition. Say 'pain' is one of the included terms only if section 6.1 lists it. Otherwise say 'reactions at the injection site' with the label's own term list.
- Rotation: credit 'change (rotate) your injection site each week' only to the single-dose pen IFU at its own URL, quoted only if it loads.
- Untagged red flags: spreading redness, warmth, pus or fever means call your prescriber.
- Allergy emergency card with the full list: swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat; trouble breathing or swallowing; severe rash or itching; fainting or feeling dizzy; very rapid heartbeat. Action: stop using it and get medical help right away, or call your local emergency number. Then 'For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.'
- Scope card: US single-dose pen; KwikPens and vials have their own leaflets.
- Leave out: technique beyond the IFU, warm-up steps, doses.
- Close with 'Not personal advice, so ask your prescriber.' and a loop line back to sentence 1. No subscribe line, no link line. 160 words or fewer.
- Post note (Exp G): target is the Pen how-to video.
plan.working_title: Tirzepatide Shot Stings for a Second: Normal? #shorts
plan.why: Visible pen 'Is this normal?' moments are our most proven Short format (279, 213, 181; 1,306 on TikTok). The angle (a sting or sore spot) differs from the bruise, blood-drop and click Shorts.

package.title: Tirzepatide Injection-Site Reaction: Something Wrong? #shorts
package.description:
The Zepbound label, from its weight-management trials, reports reactions at the injection site in 6–8% of adults on tirzepatide, by dose, vs about 2% on placebo. The label also says: rotate injection sites with each dose.
Spreading redness, warmth, pus or fever? Call your prescriber promptly.
Signs of a serious allergic reaction: swelling of the face, lips, tongue or throat; trouble breathing or swallowing; severe rash or itching; fainting or feeling dizzy; a very rapid heartbeat. Call your local emergency number. Stop using tirzepatide and get medical help right away.
For anything that isn't one of those emergency signs, don't stop or change your medicine on your own.
#Tirzepatide
Not personal advice. Talk to your doctor or prescriber about whether it's right for you.

factcheck.summary:
The Short is accurate and safe, and only two small wording fixes are needed. I checked the core claims against the DailyMed Zepbound label (revised 8/2026, updated 28 Aug 2026):
- **Injection-site reactions (Table 1):** 6% at 5 mg and 8% at both 10 mg and 15 mg, versus 2% on placebo. The table pools the two placebo-controlled weight trials, Studies 1 and 2.
- **Rotation tip:** "Rotate injection sites with each dose" is in section 2.4.

The s3 conversion is correct: 6–8% of 50 is 3–4 people, and 2% is 1.

Safety:
- s6 gives the full allergy list in the required wording. The emergency number comes first, then "Stop using tirzepatide and get medical help right away."
- s7's don't-stop line and s8's disclaimer match the fixed wording exactly.
- s5's infection red flags are general safety advice. They're correctly left without a source tag and phrased with suitable urgency.

Format: my word count is 158, which matches the post notes and fits the standard arm. There's no subscribe line and no link line. The hook is honest: it doesn't overclaim and the content pays it off.

The Lilly PDF URL loads as a real PDF of about 985 KB, but its text couldn't be extracted. The DailyMed page backs every tagged claim.
